methods.title: Methods
methods.definitions_heading: What counts as a possible zombie
methods.def_scope: Scope: persistent physical defects in the public right of way. That means potholes and roadway defects, sidewalks, streetlights, traffic signals, signs, pavement markings and street fixtures. Cases about people and complaints about private property are out.
methods.def_incident: Every closed case belongs to one incident. Cases about the same problem that were opened before the first closure are members of that incident.
methods.def_window: A report counts as a re-report when it opens after the incident closed and within {window} days of the closure, with the same kind of problem.
methods.def_place: Same place means the same street segment (no more than 75 meters apart along it), two segments that meet at the same intersection, or within {radius} meters when a case has no street segment.
methods.def_city: A planned city follow-up after a closure marked made safe, referred or planned follow-up is not a possible zombie.
methods.def_mirror: A report in the other 311 system that opened within 6 hours of the original is a mirror copy of one report, not a re-report.
methods.def_params: Parameters in this data: matching {matching}, radius {radius} meters, window {window} days.
methods.baselines_text: Some re-reports happen by chance, especially in busy places. The expected count is what chance alone would produce near each closed case. Excess is observed minus expected, with a 95% interval.
methods.excess_caption: Observed, expected and excess possible zombies by case type, headline tier
methods.excess_missing: The baseline is not part of this data yet.
methods.shift_text: Closure times were shifted at random {runs} times (seed {seed}) while locations stayed fixed. The re-reports that appear by chance are compared with the observed count.
methods.shift_range: By chance: mean {mean}; 95% of shifted runs fall between {lo} and {hi}
methods.shift_missing: The shift-test distribution is not part of this data yet.
methods.placebo_text: The baseline applied to the time-shifted closures. An excess near 0 means the baseline is not biased.
methods.placebo_missing: The placebo result is not part of this data yet.
methods.placebo_below: The placebo reads below 0 here. The baseline runs cautious, so the excess errs low and is best read as a floor.
methods.placebo_above: The placebo reads above 0 here. The baseline may run low, so the excess may read high. Read it with care.
methods.excess_floor: Read the excess as a floor where reports arrive at a steady rate. In places that get a report every month or two, the baseline expects more chance reports than it sees, so the excess reads low, not high. Where reports come in bursts or stop partway through the data, the excess can read high; the pretend-town checks below show both cases. The counts are also a floor: a possible zombie appears only when someone reports again.
methods.null_heading: Checks on pretend towns with no resurrections
methods.null_text: To test the baseline we built {towns} pretend towns where every report arrives by chance and none is a resurrection, so the true excess is 0. In none of them did the 95% interval for the excess lie above 0. It lay below 0 in {below} towns and included 0 in {covers}. In these towns every placebo warning was below 0, never above.
methods.null_caption: Excess in pretend towns with no resurrections, 300 spots each, over 1,400 days
methods.null_below_means: A reading below 0 means the baseline expected more chance reports than it saw. In these towns that is the cautious direction: the excess is understated, not overstated.
methods.null_limits: The check has limits. In a second set of {towns} pretend towns built to stress the method, {fine} were not above 0 and {above} were above 0. Those {above} had bursty reports (gaps of 10 or 200 days at random), a report every 62 days (just outside the window), a report every 75 days with closures that take 20 days, or reports that stop partway through the data. Where reports behave like that, the excess can read high. The full results are in the methods document.
methods.nt_gap30: A report at each spot every 30 days on average
methods.nt_gap45: A report at each spot every 45 days
methods.nt_gap60: A report at each spot every 60 days
methods.nt_season60: Seasonal (winter 2 times, summer a quarter), base 60 days
methods.validation_awaiting: Awaiting field labels. No precision is reported until two raters have checked a sample on the street.
methods.validation_precision: Precision {rate}, 95% interval {lo} to {hi}, from {n} rated possible zombies.
methods.validation_cant_tell: Could not tell: {share} of the sample.
methods.limit_floor: Counts are a floor: a possible zombie appears only when someone reports the problem again.
methods.limit_intersection: Matching at an intersection uses a shared segment endpoint. An endpoint is a segment break, not always a cross street.
methods.limit_origin: The new 311 system does not record who opened a case, so city staff re-reports there cannot be separated out. Those cases are shown as source unknown.
methods.status_failed: The latest run failed. The site keeps showing the last good data.
methods.report_text: Open an issue with the case numbers and what is wrong. Confirmed corrections go in the log.

score.title: Closed on time and stayed fixed
score.intro: Speed and durability side by side for each case type, with 95% intervals and the number of cases (n).
score.raw_detail: Raw stayed-fixed rate: {rate}, 95% interval {lo} to {hi}, n = {n}.
score.not_enough: Not enough cases for a rate.
score.floor: Stayed fixed counts only cases nobody reported again, so it is an upper bound on how many fixes held.
score.excess_note: A secondary check, never the headline. It is a floor in places that get a report every month or two, and it can read high where reports come in bursts.
score.excess_all: All spots: excess of {excess} re-reports (95% interval {lo} to {hi}), {observed} seen against {expected} expected, from {n} closed cases.
score.excess_without: Without bursty spots: excess of {excess} re-reports (95% interval {lo} to {hi}), {observed} seen against {expected} expected, from {n} closed cases.
score.excess_without_none: Without bursty spots: too few closed cases are left to say.
score.excess_bursty_share: {bursty} of the {n} closed cases are at spots flagged bursty: their reports come in bursts or sit in a few months.

charts.title: How long fixes last
charts.survival_intro: Share of closed cases not reported again at the same place, by days since closure. The shaded band is the 95% interval.
charts.survival_label: Survival curve for {name}, {tier}. {at7} still holding at 7 days, {at30} at 30 days, {at90} at 90 days.
charts.survival_table_caption: Share of fixes still holding, with 95% intervals
charts.no_curves: No survival curves in this data.
charts.funnel_intro: Each mark is a group, placed by how many closed cases it has (left to right) and its raw resurrection rate (up). Only groups outside the outer 99.8% limits are called unusual. Inside the limits, chance alone can produce the difference at that size.
charts.funnel_label: Funnel plot of {count} groups against the citywide rate of {rate}. {above} groups lie above the 99.8% limits and {below} below them.
charts.survival_label_base: Dashed line for {name}: {at7} at 7 days, {at30} at 30 days, {at90} at 90 days.
charts.leaderboard_intro: Groups are ordered by the shrunk rate, which pulls small groups toward the citywide rate. The raw rate and the number of cases sit beside it, so a small group never ranks on its raw rate alone.
charts.leaderboard_caption: Resurrection rate by group, shrunk toward the citywide rate
charts.intensity_note: Reporting intensity sits beside every neighborhood rate, because areas that report more show more resurrections. Counts are a floor.

deaths.heading: What the headline leaves out
deaths.intro: These counts sit outside the headline number. They are listed here so nothing is hidden.
deaths.sep_text: Cases closed as invalid or as a duplicate are reported separately and are not possible zombies. Invalid: {invalid}. Duplicate: {duplicate}.
deaths.temp_heading: How often temporary fixes come back
deaths.temp_text: Of the cases closed as made safe for now, the share reported again. Re-reports in the legacy system come from known residents. Re-reports in the new system have an unknown source and are shown in their own column.
deaths.temp_caption: Cases closed as made safe for now that were reported again, by case type
deaths.excl_fixture_note: In this preview the case counts read 0 because the sample file was filtered before it reached this site. The real export counts every excluded case by reason.
deaths.reason_unlisted_type: Case types not in the crosswalk
deaths.reason_mirror: Mirror copies across the two systems
deaths.reason_transferred_original: Originals closed as transferred or migrated (legacy system) or as Transitioned (new system)
deaths.source_unknown_text: The new 311 system has no field that says who opened a case. A re-report there after a closure marked made safe, referred or planned follow-up may be a planned city visit. The {count} possible zombies of this kind sit outside the headline count and are never added to it.
deaths.bulk_text: A department, day and closure text with at least 50 closed cases and ten times the usual daily count. A closure like this can be a paperwork cleanup, not a repair. It lowers the confidence of the possible zombies built on it and shows an orange warning on their cards.
deaths.bulk_none: No bulk-closure days in this data.
